records.themeTitle: Torah in complete clarity and Torah within earthly needs
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok distinguishes the command to rest on Shabbat and in the sabbatical year from the rarer vocation of being wholly available for Torah. The latter requires a special attainment.
records.originHebrew: וְאָמַרְנוּ, שֶׁלֹּא אָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא שֶׁאֵין עוֹשִׂין מִצְוָתוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם, רַק "רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם", וְהַיְינוּ דְּוַדַּאי לֹא צִוָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִשְׁבּוֹת כָּל הַיָּמִים, רַק לִשְׁבּוֹת בְּשַׁבָּת וּשְׁמִיטָה, וְזֶה שׁוֹמְרִין יִשְׂרָאֵל. רַק רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי אָמַר, כֵּיוָן שֶׁיָּדוּעַ שֶׁרְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הָאָדָם פָּנוּי רַק לְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה קוֹדֶם הַקִּלְקוּל שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לָאָדָם שׁוּם עֵסֶק בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְאָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי שֶׁצָּרִיךְ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם. וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סַנְהֶדְרִין צט עַמּוּד ב): "כְּשֶׁהוּא אוֹמֵר: 'לֹא יָמוּשׁ וְגוֹמֵר' – הֱוֵי אוֹמֵר לַעֲמַל תּוֹרָה נִבְרָא וְכוּלֵי, טוּבֵיהּ לִדְזָכֵי דַּהֲוֵי דְּרוֹפְתְּקֵי דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא", וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִזְכּוֹת לָזֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה דְּרוֹפְתְּקֵי דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מְיוּחָד רַק לַעֲמַל תּוֹרָה, וְזֶה נִקְרָא "עוֹשֶׂה רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם" וּמְלַאכְתּוֹ נַעֲשֵׂית עַל יְדֵי אֲחֵרִים.
records.originEnglish: We explained that the Talmud does not say they fail to perform the Omnipresent’s commandment, but that they fail to perform “the Omnipresent’s will.” God certainly did not command rest on every day, only rest on Shabbat and in the sabbatical year, and Israel observe this. But Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai said: since it is known that the Omnipresent’s will is that a person be free for words of Torah alone—as before the damage, when the human being had no occupation in the affairs of this world—an Israelite should fulfill the Omnipresent’s will. Thus the Talmud says: “When it says, ‘It shall not depart …,’ say that he was created for the toil of Torah … Fortunate is one who merits to be a vessel for the toil of Torah.” That is, one must merit this: to be a vessel for the toil of Torah, devoted solely to its labor. This is called fulfilling the Omnipresent’s will, and his work is performed by others.
records.targetHebrew: וְכֵן הַבִּיאָה לְאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, הַיְנוּ לְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל בְּצָרְכֵי הַגּוּף וְלִנְהֹג בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה מִדַּת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ כְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק כֵּיצַד מְבָרְכִין (בְּרָכוֹת דַּף ל״ה עַמּוּד ב׳). "וְלֹא נִתְּנָה תוֹרָה אֶלָּא לְאוֹכְלֵי הַמָּן" (מְכִילְתָּא פָּרָשַׁת בְּשַׁלַּח) — הַיְנוּ כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי שָׁם דִּדְבָרִים כִּכְתָבָן [סוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב — מִדַּת יוֹם, אֲבָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הִיא מִדַּת לַיְלָה, דַּרְגָּא דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כַּנּוֹדָע]. וּמָן הוּא לֶחֶם שֶׁמַּלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת אוֹכְלִין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפֶרֶק יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים (יוֹמָא דַּף ע״ה עַמּוּד ב׳), הַיְנוּ בְּלֹא שׁוּם הֲנָאָה לַגּוּף רַק לַנֶּפֶשׁ. וְלָכֵן לֹא הָיָה מִמֶּנּוּ פְּסֹלֶת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שָׁם, כִּי הָיָה כֻּלּוֹ לַהשֵּׁם. וְהַפְּסֹלֶת הוּא מִמַּה שֶּׁנִּתְכַּוֵּן לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ [דְּאִי אֶפְשָׁר בְּזוּלַת זֶה גַּם בַּאֲכִילָה, שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם נִקְרָאִים בִּלְשׁוֹן אֲכִילָה: "אָכְלָה וּמָחֲתָה פִיהָ", וְכַנּוֹדָע בְּסוֹד חֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן בַּאֲכִילָה, וְהוּא מֻשְׁרָשׁ בְּכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן לְגַמְרֵי עַד מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד]. וְלֹא יָרַד רַק "עַד בֹּאָם אֶל קְצֵה אֶרֶץ כְּנָעַן" (שְׁמוֹת ט״ז, ל״ה), כִּידוּעַ בְּסוֹד הָאָרֶץ שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם. וְהַמֶּלֶךְ הוּא שֶׁפַע כָּל מִינֵי חֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה. וְכֵן אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל נִשְׁתַּבְּחָה בְּכָל מִינֵי חֲמָדוֹת, רַק שֶׁהִיא אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהִיא אֶרֶץ הַקְּדוֹשָׁה שֶׁכָּל מִינֵי חֲמָדוֹת שֶׁלָּהּ הַכֹּל בִּקְדֻשָּׁה וְהַכָּרָה שֶׁהוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ. וְצָרִיךְ מִקּוֹדֶם שֶׁיִּבָּלְעוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בְּתוֹכָן בְּאוֹתָן אַרְבָּעִים שָׁנָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מְכִילְתָּא שָׁם).
records.targetEnglish: Likewise, entering the land of Israel means attending to bodily needs and conducting words of Torah with the ordinary way of the world, according to Rabbi Yishmael. “Torah was given only to those who ate the manna” follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, who takes the words as written: [the secret of Written Torah is the attribute of day, whereas Oral Torah is the attribute of night, the level of King David]. Manna is the bread the ministering angels eat—that is, without any enjoyment for the body, but for the soul alone. Therefore it produced no waste, as the Sages said, for it was wholly for God. Waste comes from what was intended for one’s own enjoyment [which cannot be altogether absent even in eating, for both [sexual union and eating] are called eating: “She ate and wiped her mouth”; as known concerning Adam’s sin in eating, rooted in every generation until it is fully repaired, up to Messiah son of David]. The manna descended only until “they came to the edge of the land of Canaan,” as known concerning the land, the attribute of King David and King Solomon. The king is the abundance of all kinds of worldly delights. The land of Israel too was praised for every kind of delight, but it is the land of Israel, the holy land: all its delights are in holiness and in recognition that they come from God. First the words of Torah had to be absorbed within them during those forty years, as the Sages said.
records.explanation: Dover explains the different settings of the two forms of service. Manna represents Torah without bodily self-enjoyment; entry into the land requires bringing the knowledge of God into bodily provision. This helps distinguish ordinary commanded life from the wholly Torah-centered attainment in Peri Tzadik. The requirement that Torah first be absorbed is retained, so earthly delight is not automatically identified with holy service.

records.themeTitle: Sufficiency is measured by the person’s actual need
records.themeSummary: The sages described here could live with unusually little without being distracted from Torah. Their ease with that measure is a condition of the example.
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל הֵם לֹא נִטְרְדוּ כְּלָל מִזֶּה, וְעָרַב לְרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא לְהִתְעַנּוֹת מִשַּׁבָּת לְשַׁבָּת וְגִלְגֵּל עַצְמוֹ בְּשַׁבָּת בְּקַב חֲרוּבִין, וְכֵן לְרַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָא לְהִתְאַכְזֵר עַל בְּנֵי בֵּיתוֹ כְּעוֹרֵב כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיוּ פְּנוּיִם לַעֲמַל תּוֹרָה.
records.originEnglish: But they were not troubled by this at all. Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa found it agreeable to fast from one Shabbat to the next and to make do on Shabbat with a kav of carobs; likewise Rav Adda bar Mattana, to be severe toward his household like a raven, so that they could be free for the toil of Torah.
records.targetHebrew: רַק שֶׁהוּא דַּי לוֹ בְּקַב, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ "מַשְׂבִּיעַ לְכָל חַי רָצוֹן" כְּפִי רְצוֹנוֹ, וּשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּקֵּשׁ "הַטְרִיפֵנִי לֶחֶם חֻקִּי" כְּפִי צֹרֶךְ הַלֶּחֶם שֶׁלּוֹ בִּסְעֻדַּת שְׁלֹמֹה בִּשְׁעָתָהּ, וְזֶה נֶחְשָׁב אֶצְלוֹ לְלֶחֶם חֻקִּי כְּפִי צֹרֶךְ פַּרְנָסָתוֹ, וְלֹא מוֹתָרוֹת, דְּבִקֵּשׁ עַל זֶה: "רֵישׁ וָעֹשֶׁר אַל תִּתֶּן לִי", לֹא שֶׁיֶּחְסַר לוֹ מִכְּדֵי צָרְכּוֹ וְלֹא מוֹתָרוֹת; וְאֵצֶל רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא נֶחְשָׁב קַב חֲרוּבִין לֶחֶם חֻקִּי, וְיוֹתֵר מִזֶּה הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ מוֹתָרוֹת וְעֹשֶׁר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לְבַקֵּשׁ עַל זֶה שֶׁ"אַל תִּתֶּן לִי", וְרֵישׁוּתוֹ הָיָה פָּחוֹת גַּם מִקַּב חֲרוּבִין, וְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ נִזּוֹן בִּשְׁבִילוֹ כָּל אֶחָד בְּלֶחֶם חֻקּוֹ, מִי שֶׁצָּרִיךְ כִּסְעֻדַּת שְׁלֹמֹה וְסוּס לִרְכֹּב וְעֶבֶד לָרוּץ לְפָנָיו, כָּל הִצְטָרְכוּתוֹ הוּא בִּכְלַל מְזוֹנֵי הַנִּמְשָׁךְ לְכָל אֶחָד בִּשְׁבִילוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: But a kav sufficed for him, for God “satisfies the desire of every living thing,” according to its desire. King Solomon asked, “Provide me with my allotted bread,” according to his own need for bread, in Solomon’s meal in its time. This counted for him as his allotted bread according to his need for sustenance, and not as excess, for he asked, “Give me neither poverty nor wealth”: neither less than his need nor excess. For Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, a kav of carobs counted as his allotted bread. More than that would have been excess and wealth, concerning which he should ask, “Do not give me”; his poverty would have been less even than a kav of carobs. The entire world was sustained through him, each with his allotted bread: whoever needs a meal like Solomon’s, a horse to ride, and a servant to run before him—all his requirements are included in the sustenance drawn to each person through him.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim prevents the kav of carobs from becoming a universal measure. What is excess for one person may be necessary provision for another. This explains why Peri Tzadik stresses that these sages were not troubled by their deprivation before turning, in the next paragraph, to students whose lack of food would distract them.

records.themeTitle: Rabbi Chanina’s self-restraint leaves room for others’ abundance
records.themeSummary: Rabbi Chanina’s exceptional sufficiency belongs to his own degree of closeness and service. A parallel account describes the generosity toward others expressed in that restraint.
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל הֵם לֹא נִטְרְדוּ כְּלָל מִזֶּה, וְעָרַב לְרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא לְהִתְעַנּוֹת מִשַּׁבָּת לְשַׁבָּת וְגִלְגֵּל עַצְמוֹ בְּשַׁבָּת בְּקַב חֲרוּבִין, וְכֵן לְרַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָא לְהִתְאַכְזֵר עַל בְּנֵי בֵּיתוֹ כְּעוֹרֵב כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיוּ פְּנוּיִם לַעֲמַל תּוֹרָה.
records.originEnglish: But they were not troubled by this at all. Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa found it agreeable to fast from one Shabbat to the next and to make do on Shabbat with a kav of carobs; likewise Rav Adda bar Mattana, to be severe toward his household like a raven, so that they could be free for the toil of Torah.
records.targetHebrew: ומחמת זאת ההתקרבות שהיה אצלו היה נמי בכחו לצמצם עצמו בכל הטובות שבעולם כדי שילכו לישראל יותר בשפע אף שבאמת ירדו כל הטובות רק בשבילו כ"ד בגמ' (שם) כל העולם ניזון בשביל חנינא בני וחנינא בני די לו בקב חרובין מע"ש וכו' וזה היה משום שהיה קרוב מאד להשי"ת והיה רואה היטב כמו שהוא באמת ה' אלהינו ה' אחד לכן היה בו נדיבות ענום כ"כ וכן באמת כל פרט נפש שיש בו גודל נדיבות להכנוסיא שלו יכול ג"כ לפעול בעדם כל הישועות אף למעלה מהטבע ולרמוז זאת מביא הגמרא (שם) כל המעשיות הנפלאים שהיו גבי רחב"ד
records.targetEnglish: Because of this closeness that he had, he also had the power to restrain himself concerning all the good things in the world, so that they would flow to Israel in greater abundance, although in truth all those good things descended only through him. Thus the Talmud says: “The whole world is sustained through Chanina My son, and Chanina My son is satisfied with a kav of carobs from one Shabbat ….” This was because he was very close to God and saw clearly, as it truly is, “The Lord our God, the Lord is one.” Therefore his generosity was so immense. Indeed, every individual soul that has great generosity toward its community can also bring about all their deliverances, even above nature. To indicate this, the Talmud brings all the wondrous events concerning Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim gives Rabbi Chanina’s restraint a positive communal direction: his closeness enables him to leave abundance for others. It thereby explains the conjunction of his own small portion and the whole world’s nourishment. The extraordinary power is explicitly tied to his closeness and generosity; it is not assumed of every person who consumes little.

records.themeTitle: Complete willingness must be joined to the capacity of embodied life
records.themeSummary: Rava directs students to provide for themselves when deprivation would obstruct their Torah. The higher aspiration is not a warrant to act beyond one’s actual capacity.
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לַעֲמוֹד בְּנִסָּיוֹן זֶה, הָא רָבָא בְּעַצְמוֹ אָמַר (בְּרָכוֹת שָׁם): "בְּיוֹמֵי נִיסָן וּבְיוֹמֵי תִּשְׁרֵי לָא תִּתְחֲזוּ קַמַּאי וְכוּלֵי", הֲרֵי שֶׁאַף שֶׁהָיוּ אָמוֹרָאִים וְרַבָּנָן תַּלְמִידָיו, כֵּיוָן שֶׁיָּדַע שֶׁהֶעְדֵּר הַמְּזוֹנוֹת יַטְרִיד לָהֶם, צִוָּה שֶׁיַּעַסְקוּ בְּפַרְנָסָתָם בִּימֵי נִיסָן וְתִשְׁרֵי. וְעַל זֶה מַיְירֵי הַפָּרָשָׁה: "וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ תִּשְׁמְעוּ אֶל מִצְוֺתַי וְגוֹמֵר וְאָסַפְתָּ דְגָנֶךָ וְגוֹמֵר", דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁעוֹשִׂין מִצְוֹת ה' שֶׁצִּוָּה לִשְׁבּוֹת בְּשַׁבָּת וּשְׁמִיטָה, אֲבָל אֵין עוֹשִׂין רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם לִהְיוֹת פָּנוּי רַק לַעֲמַל תּוֹרָה, וְזֶהוּ "מְלַאכְתָּן נַעֲשֵׂית עַל יְדֵי עַצְמָן". אֲבָל מִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לִהְיוֹת דְּרוֹפְתְּקֵי דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא לִהְיוֹת פָּנוּי רַק לַעֲמַל תּוֹרָה כִּרְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם, מְלַאכְתּוֹ נַעֲשֵׂית עַל יְדֵי אֲחֵרִים, וְלָאו כָּל אָדָם זוֹכֶה לָזֶה. וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: "הַרְבֵּה עָשׂוּ וְכוּלֵי כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי וְלֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדָן".
records.originEnglish: But for someone unable to withstand this trial, Rava himself said, “In the days of Nisan and the days of Tishrei, do not appear before me ….” Although they were amoraim and sages, his students, since he knew that a lack of food would distract them, he instructed them to attend to their livelihood in Nisan and Tishrei. This is the subject of the passage, “If you indeed listen to My commandments … you shall gather your grain …”: they perform God’s commandments, resting on Shabbat and in the sabbatical year as He commanded. But they do not perform the Omnipresent’s will of being free solely for the toil of Torah. This is “their work is performed by themselves.” One who merits to be a vessel for Torah’s toil, free solely for it according to the Omnipresent’s will, has his work performed by others. Not everyone merits this. Thus the Talmud says: “Many acted … according to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and did not succeed.”
records.targetHebrew: וְכָל אֶחָד צָרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן לוֹמַר פָּרָשָׁה רִאשׁוֹנָה גַּם כֵּן, שֶׁתְּחִלַּת קַבָּלָתוֹ בְּכָל יוֹם עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּעִנְיָן זֶה, גַּם לִהְיוֹת מוּפְקָר אִם יִהְיֶה רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ. רַק מִי שֶׁמַּנְהִיג בְּמִדַּת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ וְהַגְדָּרָה, הוּא מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהַרְבֵּה עָשׂוּ וְכוּלֵי וְלֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדָן, שֶׁאֵין זֶה רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ. וְכֵן אֲפִילּוּ אוֹתָם הַיְחִידִים צְרִיכִים גַּם כֵּן שֶׁיֹּאמְרוּ פָּרָשַׁת "וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְרַשְׁבִּ"י בְּשַׁבָּת (לג:) שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר לַמְּעָרָה, כִּי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת כֵּן רַק בַּמְּעָרָה וְחוּץ לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה. אֲבָל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא רוֹצֶה בְּיִשּׁוּב הָעוֹלָם, וְ"לֹא תֹהוּ בְרָאָהּ" (יְשַׁעְיָה מה, יח). וְהַנְהָגָה זוֹ לָצֵאת מִגְּבוּלוֹ וּמִכְּפִי שֶׁהוּא כְּלִי לְקַבֵּל בְּעוֹדוֹ בַּגּוּף – זֶהוּ הַנְהָגָה מֵעוֹלַם הַתֹּהוּ כַּנּוֹדָע סוֹדָם, שֶׁבִּקְּשׁוּ לְקַבֵּל שֶׁפַע אוֹר שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִכֹּחַ הַמַּגְבִּילָם הַמְּכוּנֶּה בְּשֵׁם כְּלִי. רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא בִּכְלִי הַגּוּף הַמַּגְדִּיר, אָמְרוּ (תַּעֲנִית כב:): נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתִּי בְּךָ הַחֲיֶיהָ, וְלֹא יַפְקִיר לְגַמְרֵי לָצֵאת מִגְּבוּל כְּלִי הַגּוּף; רַק צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בּוֹ כֹּחַ זוֹ שֶׁל הַהֶפְקֵר לְגַמְרֵי גַּם כֵּן; רַק אֵצֶל הַיָּחִיד זֶה בְּתֹקֶף וְלָרַבִּים זֶה, אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם כָּל אֶחָד צָרִיךְ לִשְׁנֵיהֶם.
records.targetEnglish: Everyone must also recite the first paragraph [of the Shema]: at the beginning of his daily acceptance of the kingdom of Heaven, he must be disposed in this way, even to surrender everything if this should be God’s will. A person who conducts himself according to the ordinary way of the world and within bounds does so because “many acted … and did not succeed”: this is not God’s will [for them]. Even those exceptional individuals must also recite “If you indeed listen,” just as Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai was told to return to the cave. For this is possible only in a cave, outside this world; within this world, the Holy One desires its habitation—“He did not create it for desolation.” A way of acting that goes beyond one’s bounds and beyond what one is a vessel to receive while in the body belongs to the world of chaos: they sought to receive an abundance of light beyond the limiting power called a vessel. But in this world, within the body’s limiting vessel, the Sages said, “Sustain the soul I have given you.” One must not surrender everything so as to leave the bounds of the bodily vessel. Yet the power of complete surrender must also be present. In the exceptional individual this [power] is stronger, and among the many the other [mode] is stronger; nevertheless, everyone needs both.
records.explanation: Tzidkat turns the contrast into a daily discipline represented by both paragraphs of the Shema. One accepts an unreserved willingness to serve God while preserving the bodily capacity through which service must actually occur. This explains why Rava’s instruction to work can be faithful service and why the failure of many to imitate Rabbi Shimon is a substantive qualification.

records.themeTitle: Measured service is itself desired in this world
records.themeSummary: The inability to sustain an exceptional form of self-denial changes the required practical response. Provision and composure can serve the divine will.
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לַעֲמוֹד בְּנִסָּיוֹן זֶה, הָא רָבָא בְּעַצְמוֹ אָמַר (בְּרָכוֹת שָׁם): "בְּיוֹמֵי נִיסָן וּבְיוֹמֵי תִּשְׁרֵי לָא תִּתְחֲזוּ קַמַּאי וְכוּלֵי", הֲרֵי שֶׁאַף שֶׁהָיוּ אָמוֹרָאִים וְרַבָּנָן תַּלְמִידָיו, כֵּיוָן שֶׁיָּדַע שֶׁהֶעְדֵּר הַמְּזוֹנוֹת יַטְרִיד לָהֶם, צִוָּה שֶׁיַּעַסְקוּ בְּפַרְנָסָתָם בִּימֵי נִיסָן וְתִשְׁרֵי. וְעַל זֶה מַיְירֵי הַפָּרָשָׁה: "וְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ תִּשְׁמְעוּ אֶל מִצְוֺתַי וְגוֹמֵר וְאָסַפְתָּ דְגָנֶךָ וְגוֹמֵר", דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁעוֹשִׂין מִצְוֹת ה' שֶׁצִּוָּה לִשְׁבּוֹת בְּשַׁבָּת וּשְׁמִיטָה, אֲבָל אֵין עוֹשִׂין רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם לִהְיוֹת פָּנוּי רַק לַעֲמַל תּוֹרָה, וְזֶהוּ "מְלַאכְתָּן נַעֲשֵׂית עַל יְדֵי עַצְמָן". אֲבָל מִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לִהְיוֹת דְּרוֹפְתְּקֵי דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא לִהְיוֹת פָּנוּי רַק לַעֲמַל תּוֹרָה כִּרְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם, מְלַאכְתּוֹ נַעֲשֵׂית עַל יְדֵי אֲחֵרִים, וְלָאו כָּל אָדָם זוֹכֶה לָזֶה. וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: "הַרְבֵּה עָשׂוּ וְכוּלֵי כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי וְלֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדָן".
records.originEnglish: But for someone unable to withstand this trial, Rava himself said, “In the days of Nisan and the days of Tishrei, do not appear before me ….” Although they were amoraim and sages, his students, since he knew that a lack of food would distract them, he instructed them to attend to their livelihood in Nisan and Tishrei. This is the subject of the passage, “If you indeed listen to My commandments … you shall gather your grain …”: they perform God’s commandments, resting on Shabbat and in the sabbatical year as He commanded. But they do not perform the Omnipresent’s will of being free solely for the toil of Torah. This is “their work is performed by themselves.” One who merits to be a vessel for Torah’s toil, free solely for it according to the Omnipresent’s will, has his work performed by others. Not everyone merits this. Thus the Talmud says: “Many acted … according to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and did not succeed.”
records.targetHebrew: והנה גבי שמואל הנביא מצינו שהתפללה חנה ונתתה לאמתך זרע אנשים ובארו ז"ל (ברכות לא.) זרע המובלע בין אנשים לא אריך ולא גוץ לא חכים ולא טיפש וכו' היינו שהתפללה עליו שיהיה בישוב הדעת כי בזה העולם בחר השי"ת בעבודה שהיא בישוב הדעת ולא שיבטל אדם תמיד גופו ונפשו לגמרי וכמו שמנינו באמת גבי שמואל הנביא כשאמר לו הקב"ה לך אל דוד ומשחת אותו למלך השיב שמואל איך אלך ושמע שאול והרגני וגו' וזאת התשובה שהשיב בישוב הדעת נשא חן בעיני השי"ת מאד והא ראיה שאמר לו השי"ת עצה על תשובתו והנה גבי יונה בן אמתי מצינו כששלח אותו הנביא לך ומשוח את יהוא מסר תיכף נפשו בכפו אף שהיה יותר סכנה מגבי שמואל כמבואר בפסוק שם ע"מ לא השגיח על חייו כלום להשיב איך אלך למקום סכנה כזו אכן בשמחת בית השואבה שאז עומדים ישראל בגודל אהבה ונדיבות הלב מאחד לחבירו וכאשר ישראל עומדין ביחד בגודל נדיבות אז מנהיר השי"ת ג"כ מעוצם נדיבות אהבתו לישראל לזה נבחר אז גם יונה בן אמיתי להיות נביא על ישראל אף שאהבתו היתה בהתבטלות יתירה חוץ מהגדר של סדר העולם הזה כדאיתא במכילתא יונה תבע כבוד הבן ולא תבע כבוד האב וכו' היינו שהיה תקועה בלבו בחזקה כ"כ אהבת ישראל עד שהיה תמיד תובע רק כבוד הבן ולא כבוד האב
records.targetEnglish: Concerning Samuel the prophet, we find that Hannah prayed, “Give Your maidservant offspring among men.” The Sages explained: offspring unobtrusive among men, neither tall nor short, neither wise nor foolish, and so forth. That is, she prayed that he should have composure, for in this world God chose service carried out with a settled mind, rather than a person constantly nullifying his body and soul altogether. Thus, when the Holy One told Samuel to go to David and anoint him king, Samuel answered, “How can I go? Saul will hear and kill me ….” This answer, given with composure, found great favor in God’s eyes; the proof is that God gave him counsel in response. With Jonah son of Amittai, however, when the prophet sent him to anoint Jehu, he immediately risked his life. Although the danger was greater than Samuel’s, he paid no attention to his life by asking how he could go to such a dangerous place. Yet at the rejoicing of the water drawing, when Israel stand in great love and generosity of heart toward one another, God likewise illuminates the immense generosity of His love for Israel. Jonah son of Amittai was therefore chosen then to be a prophet over Israel, although his love involved an excessive self-effacement beyond the bounds of this world’s order. As the Mekhilta states, “Jonah demanded the honor of the son and did not demand the honor of the father”: love of Israel was so firmly planted in his heart that he always demanded the son’s honor, rather than the father’s.
records.explanation: Sod distinguishes the ordinary form of service favored in this world—Samuel’s composure and attention to danger—from Jonah’s exceptional self-effacement in the setting of communal festival love. This supplies an Ishbitz account of the boundary that matters in Rav Tzadok’s discussion of livelihood. The exceptional case is retained, so “measured service” is not made into an absolute rejection of every higher degree.

records.themeTitle: Worldly activity need not reveal a preference for the temporary
records.themeSummary: The old man’s love of Shabbat shows a willingness to obey God’s command to rest. Weekday work, where work is permitted, therefore need not mean that Israel have chosen temporary life against eternal life.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁהֶרְאָה לָהֶם הַאי סָבָא עַל מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ: "מַנִּיחִין חַיֵּי עוֹלָם וְעוֹסְקִין בְּחַיֵּי שָׁעָה", שֶׁלִּכְבוֹד הַשַּׁבָּת נָקֵיט מְדָאנֵי אָסָא לְעַנֵּג הַשַּׁבָּת שֶׁנִּצְטַוּוּ לְעַנְּגוֹ; וְאָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי: "חֲזִי כַּמָּה חֲבִיבִין מִצְווֹת עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל", הַיְינוּ הַמִּצְוָה שֶׁצִּוָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לָנוּחַ בְּשַׁבָּת וְלִהְיוֹת פָּנוּי רַק לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּבְרָא הָאָדָם רַק לְשַׁמֵּשׁ אֶת קוֹנוֹ, מְדַקְדְּקִין יִשְׂרָאֵל וְחָבִיב עֲלֵיהֶם לְהוֹסִיף עֹנֶג לִכְבוֹד שַׁבָּת. וְאִם הָיָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְצַוֶּוה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל לִשְׁבּוֹת כָּל הַיָּמִים, הָיוּ שׁוֹמְעִין גַּם כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁשּׁוֹבְתִין בִּשְׁנַת הַשְּׁמִיטָה שֶׁצִּוָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לָנוּחַ מִכָּל עֲבוֹדָה; וּמִזֶּה יְתֵיב דַּעְתַּיְיהוּ בְּמַה שֶּׁעוֹסְקִין בְּחַיֵּי שָׁעָה, כֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּיתַּן רְשׁוּת לַעֲבוֹד בְּשֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה.
records.originEnglish: This is what the old man showed them in response to “They leave eternal life and occupy themselves with temporary life.” For the honor of Shabbat, he held bunches of myrtle to delight in Shabbat, which they were commanded to delight in. Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai said, “See how beloved the commandments are to Israel”: the command God gave to rest on Shabbat and be free solely for His service—as the human being was created solely to serve his Maker—is carefully observed by Israel, and they cherish adding delight for the honor of Shabbat. Had God commanded Israel to rest on every day, they would likewise obey, just as they rest during the sabbatical year, when God commanded rest from all work. This settled their minds concerning occupation with temporary life, since permission was given to work during the six days of action.

records.targetHebrew: וְזֶה הוּא מִדַּת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁלֹּא רָצָה לְהִתְפַּשֵּׁט בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּאַנְשֵׁי דוֹרוֹ, וְאַף בְּעִנְיְנֵי קְדוּשָּׁה שֶׁהִשְׁפִּיעַ לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא הָיָה מִתְפַּשֵּׁט בָּהּ, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיָה סָמוּךְ לִבּוֹ בָּטוּחַ בַּה' שֶׁנִּמְצָא אֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ קְדוּשָּׁה גְּדוֹלָה וּרְחָבָה מִנִּי יָם, גְּדוֹלָה מִמִּדַּת הַשָּׂגַת תְּפִיסַת שֵׂכֶל הָאָדָם, חַיֵּי חַיִּים עַד אֵין סוֹף וְאֵין תַּכְלִית, מַה שֶּׁאֵין בְּכֹחוֹ אַף לְצַפּוֹת וּלְקַוּוֹת לְזוֹ הַקְּדוּשָּׁה; וְנִגְלָה עָלָיו הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְאָמַר: "אֲנִי בַּעַל הַבִּירָה" – הַיְינוּ: לְךָ וּלְדוֹרוֹת הַבָּאִים שֶׁיֵּלְכוּ בְּעִקְּבוֹתֶיךָ אַרְאֶה לָהֶם שֶׁאֲנִי מַנְהִיג אֶת כָּל הָעִנְיָנִים שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם, וְאַף בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה יִמְצְאוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים; וְהוּא מִפְּנֵי שֶׁמִּצִּדְּךָ אֵינְךָ בּוֹחֵר בְּמַה שֶּׁיַּטְרִידְךָ בְּחַיֵּי שָׁעָה, לָזֶה אֶצְלְךָ הוּא רְצוֹנִי חַי בְּכָל הָעִנְיָנִים שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם.
records.targetEnglish: This was Abraham our father’s attribute: he did not wish to extend himself in the affairs of this world like the people of his generation. Even in the matters of holiness God granted him, he did not extend himself, for his heart was firm and confident in God: with God there is holiness greater and broader than the sea, greater than the measure of human apprehension—life of life without end or limit, a holiness beyond even his power to anticipate and hope for. The Holy One appeared to him and said, “I am the owner of the palace”: to you and to the generations who follow your footsteps I shall show that I govern all the world’s affairs. Even in this world’s affairs they will find words of the living God. Since, on your part, you do not choose what would distract you with temporary life, My will is alive for you in all the affairs of the world.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov distinguishes involvement in worldly affairs from choosing distraction as one’s aim. Where the person’s desire remains directed to God, divine life can be found within those affairs. This clarifies the inference Rav Tzadok draws from Shabbat: the visible weekday occupation does not by itself establish that the person prefers temporary life to service of God.

records.themeTitle: Human service strengthens the revealed divine relationship
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok applies “give strength to God” to honoring Shabbat. The qualification “as it were” matters: the claim concerns the divine relationship manifested in the world.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "וּמְדָאנֵי אָסָא לַאֲרוּס וַאֲרוּסָה", וְהוּא עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּגְּמָרָא: "חַד כְּנֶגֶד זָכוֹר וְחַד כְּנֶגֶד שָׁמוֹר", וּבָרַמְבַּ"ן יִתְרוֹ כָּתַב בְּשֵׁם סֵפֶר הַבָּהִיר, דְּ"שָׁמוֹר" הִיא שַׁבָּת מַלְכְּתָא, וְ"זָכוֹר" כְּנֶגֶד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְזֶהוּ "לַאֲרוּס וַאֲרוּסָה". וְאָמַר: "לְאִתְקָפָא חַלָּשִׁין", וְהַיְינוּ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי שֶׁהוּא חָלוּשׁ בְּדַעְתּוֹ עַל מַה שֶּׁטָּרוּד בִּימֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה. וְאָמַר מִקּוֹדֶם "לַאֲרוּס וַאֲרוּסָה", עַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "תְּנוּ עֹז לֵאלֹהִים", שֶׁעַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁעוֹשִׂין לִכְבוֹד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָהֲבִין תּוּקְפָא וְחֵילָא כִּבְיָכוֹל לְקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב, לב סוֹף עַמּוּד ב), וְזֶהוּ "לְאִתְקָפָא חַלָּשִׁין".
records.originEnglish: This is “and bunches of myrtle for groom and bride,” following the Talmud’s “one corresponding to ‘Remember’ and one to ‘Observe.’” Ramban in Yitro writes in the name of Sefer HaBahir that “Observe” is the Shabbat queen, while “Remember” corresponds to the blessed God. This is “for groom and bride.” It says, “to strengthen the weak”: the Israelite whose spirit is weakened by being occupied with this world’s affairs during the days of action. First it says, “for groom and bride,” even in the likeness of “Give strength to God”: through what they do for God’s honor, they give strength and power, as it were, to the Holy One, as stated in the holy Zohar. This is “to strengthen the weak.”
records.targetHebrew: וְ"אִם צָדַקְתָּ מַה תִּתֶּן לוֹ" [אִיּוֹב ל״ה:ז׳], כְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא (שְׁמִינִי [סִימָן ח׳]): מָה אִכְפַּת לֵיהּ לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בֵּין שׁוֹחֵט מִן הַצַּוָּאר וְכוּלֵי, לָכֵן "שְׂכַר מִצְוָה — מִצְוָה". אֲבָל בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר אָמְרוּ: "תְּנוּ עֹז לֵאלֹהִים" [תְּהִלִּים ס״ח:ל״ה], וּכְשֶׁחַס וְשָׁלוֹם חוֹטֵא — מַתִּישׁ כֹּחַ פַּמַּלְיָא שֶׁל מַעְלָה; וְאִם כֵּן דִּינוֹ כְּשׂוֹכֵר לַעֲשׂוֹת בְּשֶׁלּוֹ, דְּנוֹתֵן שְׂכָרוֹ מִשָּׁלֵם. וּשְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת: הָרִאשׁוֹן — בְּעַצְמוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ; וְהַשֵּׁנִי — בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִדּוֹתָיו, וְהוּא הַנִּקְרָא בְּרַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה "שְׁכִינָה", כְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (סַנְהֶדְרִין מ״ו עַמּוּד א׳): כְּשֶׁאָדָם חוֹטֵא, שְׁכִינָה מָה אוֹמֶרֶת? "קַלַּנִי מֵרֹאשִׁי וְכוּלֵי". וְזֶהוּ: "וְנֶהֱנִין מִזִּיו הַשְּׁכִינָה" [בְּרָכוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳]:
records.targetEnglish: “If you are righteous, what do you give Him?” As Midrash Tanchuma says: What difference does it make to the Holy One whether one slaughters from the neck …? Therefore, “The reward of a commandment is a commandment.” Elsewhere, however, they said, “Give strength to God”; and when, God forbid, someone sins, he weakens the strength of the heavenly retinue. It is then like one who hires someone to work on his own property and pays his full wage. Both are true: the first concerns His essence, and the second the extension of His attributes, which the Sages call the Shekhinah. Thus the Talmud says: When a person sins, what does the Shekhinah say? “My head is heavy ….” This is “They enjoy the radiance of the Shekhinah.”
records.explanation: Kometz states the distinction that keeps Rav Tzadok’s expression precise. God’s essence gains nothing from human action, while the manifestation of the divine attributes—the Shekhinah—stands in a real relationship with that action. Thus honoring Shabbat can be described as giving strength without implying an independent bodily weakness in God.

records.themeTitle: Renewal belongs to the creature’s recognition
records.themeSummary: The language of giving strength names a response from below to the divine source. A related account locates renewal in the created recipient’s recognition.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר: "וּמְדָאנֵי אָסָא לַאֲרוּס וַאֲרוּסָה", וְהוּא עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּגְּמָרָא: "חַד כְּנֶגֶד זָכוֹר וְחַד כְּנֶגֶד שָׁמוֹר", וּבָרַמְבַּ"ן יִתְרוֹ כָּתַב בְּשֵׁם סֵפֶר הַבָּהִיר, דְּ"שָׁמוֹר" הִיא שַׁבָּת מַלְכְּתָא, וְ"זָכוֹר" כְּנֶגֶד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְזֶהוּ "לַאֲרוּס וַאֲרוּסָה". וְאָמַר: "לְאִתְקָפָא חַלָּשִׁין", וְהַיְינוּ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי שֶׁהוּא חָלוּשׁ בְּדַעְתּוֹ עַל מַה שֶּׁטָּרוּד בִּימֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה. וְאָמַר מִקּוֹדֶם "לַאֲרוּס וַאֲרוּסָה", עַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "תְּנוּ עֹז לֵאלֹהִים", שֶׁעַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁעוֹשִׂין לִכְבוֹד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָהֲבִין תּוּקְפָא וְחֵילָא כִּבְיָכוֹל לְקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב, לב סוֹף עַמּוּד ב), וְזֶהוּ "לְאִתְקָפָא חַלָּשִׁין".
records.originEnglish: This is “and bunches of myrtle for groom and bride,” following the Talmud’s “one corresponding to ‘Remember’ and one to ‘Observe.’” Ramban in Yitro writes in the name of Sefer HaBahir that “Observe” is the Shabbat queen, while “Remember” corresponds to the blessed God. This is “for groom and bride.” It says, “to strengthen the weak”: the Israelite whose spirit is weakened by being occupied with this world’s affairs during the days of action. First it says, “for groom and bride,” even in the likeness of “Give strength to God”: through what they do for God’s honor, they give strength and power, as it were, to the Holy One, as stated in the holy Zohar. This is “to strengthen the weak.”
records.targetHebrew: ועל זה נאמר תקעו בחדש שופר וגו' והוא ע"ד הכתוב תנו עוז לאלהים וכמבואר בזוה"ק (בא לב) יהבין תוקפא וחילא לקב"ה וכו' כי בר"ה נתעורר בחזרה ההתחדשות וזאת היא רק מצד הבריאה כי מצדו ית' אין שייך שום התחדשות כיון שאינו מתיישן מצדו שום דבר כדאי' בגמ' (יבמות טז:) פסוק זה שר עולם אמרו נער הייתי גם זקנתי וכי תימא קב"ה מי איכא זקנה קמי קב"ה וכו' ושר עולם היינו זאת הנקודה שהניח השי"ת בכל הבריאה שתכיר דלית לה מגרמיה שום כח ועל אותה הנקודה אמרו ז"ל אין לך עשב מלמטה שאין לו מזל מלמעלה וכו' וזאת ההכרה הוא באמת עיקר הכח מהבריאה כדאיתא בזוה"ק (פנחס רנז:)
records.targetEnglish: Concerning this it says, “Sound the shofar at the new moon …,” in the manner of “Give strength to God,” as explained in the holy Zohar: “They give strength and power to the Holy One ….” On Rosh Hashanah renewal is awakened again. This is only from the side of creation, for from His side no renewal applies, since nothing grows old from His side. Thus the Talmud says that the prince of the world said the verse, “I was young, and have also grown old”: could one say it was the Holy One—does old age apply to Him? The prince of the world is the point God placed in all creation, that it should recognize it has no power of its own. Concerning that point the Sages said, “There is no blade of grass below that has no mazal above ….” This recognition is, in truth, creation’s essential strength, as stated in the holy Zohar.
records.explanation: Sod explains the strengthening from the recipient’s side: recognizing the divine source renews the creature’s own power. Together with Rav Tzadok’s Shabbat application, it shows why honoring God can strengthen the discouraged person. The Rosh Hashanah setting is preserved as a comparison; the target does not claim to explain the myrtle ritual itself.

records.themeTitle: Wine consoles a joy that has been damaged
records.themeSummary: The “mourners” are the person’s own limbs after sin. The wine’s proper joy belongs to the restoration of an upright heart.
records.originHebrew: אַךְ הָעִנְיָן עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "דְּרָכָיו רָאִיתִי וְאֶרְפָּאֵהוּ, וְאַשְׁלֵם נִחוּמִים לוֹ וְלַאֲבֵלָיו", וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה טז): "אֵלּוּ אֵבָרָיו הַמִּתְאַבְּלִין עָלָיו"; וּבְרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא (חֵלֶק ג, קכג עַמּוּד א) אַחַר שֶׁהֶאֱרִיךְ בְּעִנְיַן הַתְּשׁוּבָה, אִיתָא: "וְכָל פִּקּוּדִין דַּעֲשֵׂה דַּהֲווֹ עֲתִידִין לְשַׁרְיָא בִּרְמַ"ח אֵבָרִין דִּילֵיהּ כֻּלְּהוּ מִתְאַבְּלִין עֲלֵיהּ, וְרָזָא דְּמִלָּה 'דְּרָכָיו רָאִיתִי וְגוֹמֵר וְלַאֲבֵלָיו' – אִלֵּין רְמַ"ח אֵיבָרִין דְּקָא מִתְאַבְּלָן עֲלֵיהּ וְכוּלֵי". וְזֶה כַּוָּנַת הַגְּמָרָא "לֹא נִבְרָא יַיִן אֶלָּא לְנַחֵם אֲבֵלִים", שֶׁאַחַר הַקִּלְקוּל נִבְרָא הַיַּיִן לְשַׂמֵּחַ הַלֵּב; וְהוּא עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר (תַּעֲנִית טו עַמּוּד א): "'יְשָׁרִים לְשִׂמְחָה' – לִישְׁרֵי לֵב שִׂמְחָה", וְהַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁזּוֹכִין לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב זוֹכִין לְשִׂמְחָה, וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא: "זָכָה מְשַׂמְּחוֹ", דִּכְתִיב: "וְיַיִן יְשַׂמַּח לְבַב אֱנוֹשׁ".
records.originEnglish: The matter follows the verse, “I have seen his ways and will heal him … and repay consolations to him and to his mourners.” Midrash Rabbah explains: these are his limbs, which mourn over him. Raaya Meheimna, after an extended account of repentance, states: “All the positive commandments that were destined to rest in his 248 limbs—all mourn over him. The secret of the matter is ‘I have seen his ways … and to his mourners’: these are the 248 limbs that mourn over him ….” This is the Talmud’s meaning, “Wine was created only to console mourners”: after the damage, wine was created to gladden the heart. Thus the Talmud says, “‘The upright for joy’—joy for the upright of heart.” When people merit to straighten the heart, they merit joy. This is “If he merits, it gladdens him,” as it is written, “Wine gladdens the human heart.”
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶהוּ שֶׁהוּזְהַר אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, כִּי ״הָאֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר״ (קֹהֶלֶת ז:כט) וְכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ קוֹמָה אַחַת שְׁלֵימָה וְכַאֲשֶׁר הַקּוֹמָה בִּשְׁלֵימוּת, אֵין צָרִיךְ לְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל עַל אַהֲבַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת בַּלֵּב, שֶׁהֲרֵי בַּטֶּבַע הוּא כָּךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָאָדָם אוֹהֵב אֶת אֵבְרֵי גּוּפוֹ וְ״לֹא נִבְרָא יַיִן אֶלָּא לְנַחֵם אֲבֵלִים וְכוּלֵיהּ״ (עֵירוּבִין ס״ה עַמּוּד א׳) הַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי שֶׁיֵּשׁ צַעַר וְצָרָה בָּעוֹלָם צָרִיךְ לְבַקֵּשׁ שִׂמְחָה: ״[יִשְׁתֶּה] וְיִשְׁכַּח רִישׁוֹ״ (מִשְׁלֵי ל״א:ז׳) אֲבָל מִי שֶׁבְּשִׂמְחָה, אֵין לוֹ לְבַקֵּשׁ תּוֹסֶפֶת שִׂמְחָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כָּל זְמַן שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לֹא שָׂמַח בְּעוֹלָמוֹ שִׂמְחָה שְׁלֵימָה עַל יְדֵי קִיּוּם אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן מִצְוָתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לְבַקֵּשׁ וּלְהִתְאַוּוֹת לְתוֹסֶפֶת שִׂמְחָה מַה שֶּׁאֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹתֵן לוֹ
records.targetEnglish: This is what Adam was warned about, for “God made the human being upright.” The whole world is one complete body. When the body is complete, there is no need to work to bring love of other creatures into the heart: it is natural, just as a person loves the limbs of his body. “Wine was created only to console mourners …” means that, because there are pain and trouble in the world, one needs to seek joy—“Let him drink and forget his poverty.” But someone who is already joyful should not seek added joy in this world while the Holy One has not rejoiced in His world with complete joy through Adam’s fulfillment of his commandment: not to seek and desire added joy that God does not give him.
records.explanation: Machshavot explains why consolation is a post-damage need. An upright and integrated human life already has a natural love and joy; trouble creates the need to restore it. This gives the broader logic for Rav Tzadok’s identification of the grieving limbs, while preserving the distinction between restorative joy and seeking an unnecessary addition that itself produces damage.

records.themeTitle: Rest can be a foretaste of the repaired life
records.themeSummary: Shabbat gives a present measure of the future rest: relief from the sadness and conflict of the weekday struggle. A related account describes Jacob tasting that rest through the old wine sent by Joseph.
records.originHebrew: וְשַׁבָּת הוּא "מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרָכוֹת נז עַמּוּד ב), וְכֵן נִדְרָשׁ (בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ חֵלֶק א, מח עַמּוּד ב): "'בְּיוֹם הָנִיחַ ה' לְךָ מֵעָצְבְּךָ וּמֵרָגְזֶךָ' – עַל יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת", שֶׁאָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹתֵן נִיחָא בְּלֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל מַה שֶּׁהוּא עָצֵב מִמַּה שֶּׁהָיָה מְשׁוּקָּע בִּימֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וּמֵהָרוֹגֶז וּמֵהַחֲרָדָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ מִמִּלְחֶמֶת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע. וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "וַאֲשַׁלֵּם נִחֻמִים לוֹ וְלַאֲבֵלָיו" – אֵלּוּ רְמַ"ח אֵבָרִים הַמִּתְאַבְּלִים עָלָיו.
records.originEnglish: Shabbat is “a likeness of the World to Come.” Thus the holy Zohar expounds “On the day the Lord gives you rest from your sorrow and agitation” concerning Shabbat. Then God gives rest in the Israelite heart from its sadness over having been immersed in this world’s affairs during the days of action, and from the agitation and fear of its struggle with the evil inclination. Concerning this it says, “I will repay consolations to him and to his mourners”: these are the 248 limbs that mourn over him.
records.targetHebrew: וְאָז שָׁלַח לְאָבִיו: ״יַיִן יָשָׁן שֶׁדַּעַת זְקֵנִים נוֹחָה הֵימֶנּוּ״ (מְגִלָּה ט״ז עַמּוּד ב׳) ״יָשָׁן״ הַיְינוּ מֵאוֹתוֹ הַמְשׁוּמָּר בַּעֲנָבָיו וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (מ׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): לְאָדָם שֶׁטּוֹב — מַטְעִימִין [מִפֵּירוֹת מַעֲשָׂיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה] וּכְעִנְיַן: ״עוֹלָמְךָ תִּרְאֶה בְחַיֶּיךָ״ (בְּרָכוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳) וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (תַּנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פֶּרֶק ה׳) עַל פָּסוּק ״וַיְחִי יַעֲקֹב״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית מ״ז:כ״ח): שֶׁזָּכָה לְחַיִּים שֶׁלֹּא בְּצַעַר וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּיֵצֶר הָרָע וְלֹא בְּחִנָּם בִּקֵּשׁ לֵישֵׁב בְּשַׁלְוָה, וְלֹא בִּקֵּשׁ דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין שַׁיָּיךְ לוֹ, רַק שֶׁעַדַיִין לֹא הִגִּיעַ זְמַנּוֹ אֲבָל סוֹף זָכָה לֵישֵׁב בְּשַׁלְוָה כְּשֶׁרָאָה מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה וְלֹא מֵת כְּלָל וְזֶהוּ ״הַיַּיִן יָשָׁן שֶׁדַּעַת זְקֵנִים״ — אַחַר שֶׁפָּסַק מֵהֶם כָּל חֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק ״וַאדֹנִי זָקֵן״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית י״ח:י״ב) — ״נוֹחָה״ הַיְינוּ שֶׁמּוֹצְאִים הַנַּיְיחָא שֶׁלָּהֶם רַק כַּאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ בְּדַעְתָּם הַשָּׂגַת הַשִּׂמְחָה שְׁלֵימָה דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
records.targetEnglish: Then he sent his father “old wine, in which the mind of the aged finds rest.” “Old” means from that wine preserved in its grapes, in the manner of the Sages’ statement, “A person who is good is given a taste [of the fruits of his deeds in this world],” and “May you see your world in your lifetime.” Thus they said concerning “Jacob lived” that he merited a life without pain and without the evil inclination. His request to dwell in tranquillity was not in vain, nor did he seek something that did not belong to him; its time had simply not yet arrived. In the end he merited to dwell in tranquillity when he saw his offspring complete, and he did not die at all. This is “the old wine, in which the mind of the aged”—after all worldly desires have ceased from them, as Bereshit Rabbah says concerning “my lord is old”—“finds rest”: they find their rest only when God grants their mind an apprehension of the complete joy of this world.
records.explanation: Machshavot supplies a narrative example of a future kind of rest tasted within life. Jacob’s earlier desire for tranquillity becomes fulfilled at its proper time, with reconciliation and completeness. This sharpens Peri Tzadik’s “likeness of the World to Come”: the Shabbat rest is not merely interruption of labor but a taste of life relieved of the inner conflict that labor and desire have carried.

records.themeTitle: Consolation must reach the earlier fear as well as the future
records.themeSummary: The rest of Shabbat consoles the person about what has already troubled the heart. Future relief alone would leave the earlier fear unanswered.
records.originHebrew: וְשַׁבָּת הוּא "מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרָכוֹת נז עַמּוּד ב), וְכֵן נִדְרָשׁ (בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ חֵלֶק א, מח עַמּוּד ב): "'בְּיוֹם הָנִיחַ ה' לְךָ מֵעָצְבְּךָ וּמֵרָגְזֶךָ' – עַל יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת", שֶׁאָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹתֵן נִיחָא בְּלֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל מַה שֶּׁהוּא עָצֵב מִמַּה שֶּׁהָיָה מְשׁוּקָּע בִּימֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וּמֵהָרוֹגֶז וּמֵהַחֲרָדָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ מִמִּלְחֶמֶת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע. וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "וַאֲשַׁלֵּם נִחֻמִים לוֹ וְלַאֲבֵלָיו" – אֵלּוּ רְמַ"ח אֵבָרִים הַמִּתְאַבְּלִים עָלָיו.
records.originEnglish: Shabbat is “a likeness of the World to Come.” Thus the holy Zohar expounds “On the day the Lord gives you rest from your sorrow and agitation” concerning Shabbat. Then God gives rest in the Israelite heart from its sadness over having been immersed in this world’s affairs during the days of action, and from the agitation and fear of its struggle with the evil inclination. Concerning this it says, “I will repay consolations to him and to his mourners”: these are the 248 limbs that mourn over him.
records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 17:1
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶה הוּא בְּרָזָא דִּכְפִילָא, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה בּוֹנֶה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ טוֹבָה כְּפוּלָה, שֶׁאַחַר זֶה לֹא יִצְרַךְ עוֹד לְיִרְאָה מוּפְלֶגֶת, וְגַם שְׂכָרוֹ יִתֵּן לוֹ בְּכֶפֶל עַל יְדֵי זֶה שֶׁהָיָה בּוֹ עַד עַתָּה יִרְאָה גְּדוֹלָה כָּל כָּךְ. כִּי אִם לֹא הָיָה מַרְאֶה לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רַק מִכָּאן וּלְהַבָּא וְלֹא עַל הֶעָבָר, אֲזַי לֹא הָיָה בְּנַיְיחָא עוֹד עַל הֶעָבָר לָמָּה הוּצְרַךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּיִרְאָה כָּל כָּךְ, לָזֶה יְשַׁלֵּם לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׂכֻּרְתּוֹ כְּפוּלָה עַל הֶעָבָר וְלֶעָתִיד.
records.targetEnglish: This is the secret of doubling: through it God builds a double good. Afterward the person will no longer need such extraordinary fear, and God will also give him double reward for having had such great fear until now. If God showed him only what would be from now onward, and not concerning the past, he would still have no rest about the past—why he had needed to be in such great fear. Therefore God pays him double recompense, concerning the past and the future.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains what it means for consolation to address the past itself: the earlier fear must receive an answer, beyond the promise that fear will stop. Its surrounding paragraph relates this double good to Shabbat and the coming world’s rest. This illuminates Rav Tzadok’s precise emphasis on relief from the heart’s sadness about the weekday life already lived.

records.themeTitle: Bodily nourishment can clarify or obstruct the mind
records.themeSummary: Rav Nachman’s wine is presented as a means of restoring clarity in a mixed and damaged condition. The manner of receiving bodily nourishment determines its spiritual effect.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן מַה שֶּׁאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן דְּכָל כַּמָּה דְּלָא שָׁתֵינָא רְבִיעֲתָא דְּחַמְרָא לָא צִילָאי דַּעְתַּאי, הוּא גַּם כֵּן אַחַר הַקִּלְקוּל שֶׁנִּצְרַךְ הַיַּיִן לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב וּלְשַׂמְּחוֹ, וְקוֹדֶם הָעִרְבּוּב טוֹב וָרָע לֹא הָיָה נִצְרַךְ הַיַּיִן כְּלָל.
records.originEnglish: Likewise, Rav Nachman’s statement that his mind was not clear until he drank a quarter-log of wine also concerns the state after the damage, when wine was needed to straighten the heart and gladden it. Before the mixture of good and evil, wine was not needed at all.
records.targetHebrew: וְשֶׁמֶן, הָרוֹמֵז לְחָכְמָה שֶׁהִיא הַיְּדִיעָה וְהַכָּרָה הַבְּרוּרָה שֶׁ"אֲנִי אֱלֹהֵיכֶם", זֶה בָּא אַחַר הָאֲכִילָה הַהֲגוּנָה כָּרָאוּי לְשֵׁם ה', כְּדֵי לְהַחֲיוֹת נַפְשׁוֹ, אָז מוֹסֶפֶת לוֹ חָכְמָה וְדַעַת ה' אַחַר כָּךְ; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֲכִילָה גַּסָּה כִּבְהֵמָה מְטַמְטֶמֶת הַלֵּב וְהַמֹּחַ, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא קַמָּא ע״ב עַמּוּד א׳): "הַאי דְּלָא אֲמָרִי לָךְ וְכוּלֵי — דְּלָא אֲכַלִי בִּשְׂרָא דְּתוֹרָא".
records.targetEnglish: Oil, which alludes to wisdom—the clear knowledge and recognition that “I am your God”—comes after proper eating, as is fitting for God’s sake, to sustain one’s soul. Then it adds wisdom and knowledge of God afterward. Gross eating like an animal, however, dulls the heart and mind. Thus the Sages said: “The reason I did not tell you … was that I had not eaten beef.”
records.explanation: Et HaOchel explains the condition under which food helps understanding rather than dulling it: its reception must serve life before God. The example of beef parallels Rav Nachman’s use of wine as a support for clarity. Peri Tzadik adds the historical claim that such restoration was unnecessary before the mixture of good and evil; Et HaOchel does not make that claim in this excerpt.

records.themeTitle: Attention turns the cup toward the joy of a commandment
records.themeSummary: The spiritual use of wine requires a clarified relation to it. Its ordinary tendency to make a person forget is not itself the holy clarity Rav Tzadok describes.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן מַה שֶּׁאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן דְּכָל כַּמָּה דְּלָא שָׁתֵינָא רְבִיעֲתָא דְּחַמְרָא לָא צִילָאי דַּעְתַּאי, הוּא גַּם כֵּן אַחַר הַקִּלְקוּל שֶׁנִּצְרַךְ הַיַּיִן לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב וּלְשַׂמְּחוֹ, וְקוֹדֶם הָעִרְבּוּב טוֹב וָרָע לֹא הָיָה נִצְרַךְ הַיַּיִן כְּלָל.
records.originEnglish: Likewise, Rav Nachman’s statement that his mind was not clear until he drank a quarter-log of wine also concerns the state after the damage, when wine was needed to straighten the heart and gladden it. Before the mixture of good and evil, wine was not needed at all.
records.targetHebrew: וזהו נמי מה שאמרו ז"ל בגמ' על כוס של ברכה שצריך האדם ליתן עיניו בו וגם כל הקדושות אומרים דוקא על כוס יין והוא כי כוס של ברכה רומז נמי למדת מלכות שמים דלית ליה עיינין ולכך צריכין ליתן עיניו בו, היינו להעמיק ולהכניס בו עיינין וגם המצוה הוא דוקא על יין כי יין משכח דעת האדם לכך כשיעמיק האדם ויכניס בהכוס יין עיינין אזי ימצא בזה היין בעצמו שמחה של מצוה,
records.targetEnglish: This is also what the Sages said concerning the cup of blessing: a person must set his eyes upon it, and all sanctifications are recited specifically over a cup of wine. The cup of blessing also alludes to the attribute of the kingdom of Heaven, which has no eyes; therefore one must set one’s eyes upon it—that is, look deeply and bring eyes into it. The commandment is specifically with wine because wine makes a person forget his understanding. When a person looks deeply and brings eyes into the cup of wine, he will find in this very wine the joy of a commandment.
records.explanation: Sod names the deliberate attention required within the cup ritual: the same wine that can make a person forget can become the setting of a commandment’s joy. This illuminates the quality of the clarity discussed by Rav Tzadok without treating the bodily effect of wine as automatically holy or supplying an unquoted theory of the pre-sin state.

records.themeTitle: A blessing recognizes that the good remains in the Giver’s hand
records.themeSummary: The Grace after Meals protects eating through the recognition of the One who gives it. The person’s benefit need not become a claim of independent possession.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן אַחַר שֶׁסּוֹעֵד, דְּאִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא יב עַמּוּד ב): "אַחַר שֶׁאוֹכֵל וְשׁוֹתֶה אֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא לֵב אֶחָד", וְלֹא נִתְפָּרֵשׁ אֵיזֶה לֵב אֶחָד, שֶׁמִּקּוֹדֶם שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שְׁנֵי לְבָבוֹת, הַיְינוּ יֵצֶר טוֹב וְיֵצֶר רָע, וּלְאַחַר שֶׁאָכַל וְשָׁתָה, אִם הָיְתָה אֲכִילָתוֹ בִּקְדוּשָׁה, יֵשׁ לוֹ רַק לֵב אֶחָד לַאֲבִיהוּ שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הָאֲכִילָה בִּקְדוּשָׁה מְתַקֵּן הַפְּגָם שֶׁהָיָה בָּאֲכִילָה; וְאִם חַס וְשָׁלוֹם הָאֲכִילָה לְשֵׁם תַּאֲוָה, אָז עַל יְדֵי הָאֲכִילָה גּוֹרֵם קִטְרוּג יֵצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁאֵין יֵצֶר הָרָע שׁוֹלֵט אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ בְּסִפְרֵי מִכַּמָּה פְסוּקִים. וְעַל יְדֵי בִּרְכַּת הַמָּזוֹן שֶׁמְּבָרֵךְ אַחַר אֲכִילָתוֹ פּוֹעֵל שֶׁלֹּא יַזִּיק אֲכִילָתוֹ, כֵּיוָן שֶׁמַּכִּיר כֹּחַ הַנּוֹתֵן, וּכְשֶׁבָּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵינוֹ גוֹרֵם קִטְרוּג יֵצֶר הָרָע. וְכֵן דָּרְשׁוּ (בְּרָכוֹת נג עַמּוּד ב): "'וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם' – אֵלּוּ מַיִם רִאשׁוֹנִים, 'וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים' – אֵלּוּ מַיִם אַחֲרוֹנִים וְכוּלֵי", וְכָל זֶה עֵצָה שֶׁתִּהְיֶה הָאֲכִילָה בִּקְדוּשָׁה.
records.originEnglish: Likewise after a meal: the Talmud says, “After a person eats and drinks, he has only one heart.” It does not specify which one heart. Beforehand he has two hearts, the good inclination and the evil inclination. After he eats and drinks, if his eating was in holiness, he has only one heart toward his Father in heaven, for through holy eating he repairs the damage that came through eating. But if, God forbid, his eating is for the sake of desire, his eating gives rise to the evil inclination’s accusation; the evil inclination gains control through eating and drinking, as the Sifrei derives from several verses. Through the Grace after Meals that he recites after eating, he brings it about that his eating does no harm, because he recognizes the power of the Giver. When it comes from the blessed God, it does not give rise to the evil inclination’s accusation. So they expounded: “Sanctify yourselves”—the first washing of the hands; “and you shall be holy”—the final washing, and so forth. All this is counsel that eating should take place in holiness.

records.targetEnglish: Thus the Talmud states: Rabbi Levi raised a contradiction: it is written, “The earth and its fullness belong to the Lord,” and it is written, “He has given the earth to human beings.” There is no difficulty: one is before a blessing, the other after a blessing. “After a blessing” indicates that the person recognizes God is the giver of the good and the good remains in His hand. records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef makes the recognition of the Giver more exact: receiving good does not mean that it has passed outside God’s domain. records.themeTitle: The second inclination’s powers can be brought into service
records.themeSummary: The joy of the cup and song belongs to the straightened heart, in which both inclinations are directed toward good. This is more than leaving the second inclination unused.

records.originEnglish: Therefore the commandment is to bless over a cup of wine to gladden the heart, so that there is “joy for the upright of heart”: when one merits to empty evil from the fool’s heart and straighten the heart. records.targetEnglish: One who conducts himself in holiness even in all permitted matters and bodily needs—that is, all his actions are for Heaven, and he brings God’s service and will into them, as the Sages said concerning Hillel and Shammai—is called a hasid, a pious person. That means he does not merely adhere to the strict line of law. This is “With all your heart”—with both your inclinations. A righteous person subdues his inclination, but this person brings holiness also into all the inclination’s desires. Then God, measure for measure, places holiness in all he does, and he merits to bring forth much holiness specifically from the evil inclination. It is then called “very good,” more than simply good. Concerning this it says, “Where penitents stand, the wholly righteous cannot ….” God arranges missteps and obstacles for him, and he needs repentance and atonement for them, for they are called sin; through this he brings the precious forth from the base.
records.explanation: Tzidkat explains the difference between subduing a power and bringing that power into service. This gives content to Peri Tzadik’s “two hearts” becoming one heart for good: bodily desire can be redirected rather than merely suppressed. The target’s qualification is retained in the quotation: missteps remain sin requiring repentance and atonement; their eventual repair does not make them permissible.

records.themeTitle: Thanksgiving remains for the deliverance from the inclination
records.themeSummary: The continuing thanksgiving offering does not contradict the cessation of offerings that repair damage. It acknowledges the deliverance through which that repaired state was attained.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן מִצְוַת נְסָכִים מוֹרָה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּשִׂמְחָה וְנִיחָא מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, וְזֶה נִצְרַךְ רַק אַחַר הַקִּלְקוּל; אֲבָל קוֹדֶם הַקִּלְקוּל לֹא נִצְרְכוּ כְּלָל לְקָרְבָּנוֹת, שֶׁהֲרֵי קָרְבָּן רִאשׁוֹן שֶׁהִקְרִיב אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן הָיָה רַק אַחַר שֶׁאָמַר: "שֶׁבִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁסָּרַחְתִּי עוֹלָם חָשַׁךְ בַּעֲדִי וְכוּלֵי, כֵּיוָן שֶׁעָלָה עַמּוּד הַשַּׁחַר וְכוּלֵי עָמַד וְהִקְרִיב וְכוּלֵי", וְכֵן נֹחַ הִקְרִיב הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת אַחַר הַמַּבּוּל. וּלְעָתִיד כָּל הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת בְּטֵלִין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט), וְקָרְבַּן תּוֹדָה שֶׁאֵינוֹ בָּטֵל הוּא גַּם כֵּן לְהוֹדוֹת עַל נֵס שֶׁנִּיצוֹל מִצָּרָה; וְקוֹדֶם הַקִּלְקוּל לֹא הָיָה צָרִיךְ כְּלָל קָרְבָּן, וְלֹא הָיָה נְסָכִים כְּלָל, הַנְּסָכִים בָּאוּ רַק לְהָבִיא שִׂמְחָה. כִּי כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם מַר נֶפֶשׁ, כִּבְיָכוֹל אֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּנִיחָא, וְאַחַר שֶׁמְּתַקֵּן מֵבִיא נְסָכִים שֶׁאָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּנִיחָא; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן קוֹדֶם הַקִּלְקוּל לֹא הָיָה נִצְרַךְ כְּלָל לְיַיִן, וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא יַיִן רַק לְנַחֵם אֲבֵלִים וְכוּלֵי".
records.originEnglish: The commandment of libations likewise indicates that God has joy and rest from Israel. This is needed only after the damage; before the damage, offerings were not needed at all. Adam’s first offering was only after he said, “Because I sinned, the world has grown dark on my account …,” and, when dawn came, he arose and offered. Noah likewise offered after the Flood. In the future all offerings cease, as stated in Vayikra Rabbah. The thanksgiving offering, which does not cease, likewise gives thanks for a miracle by which one escaped trouble. Before the damage there was no need for an offering, nor for libations: libations came only to bring joy. When a person is embittered, God, as it were, is not at rest; after the person makes repair, he brings libations, and then God is at rest. Before the damage, however, wine was not needed at all. This is “Wine was created only to console mourners ….”

records.targetEnglish: Concerning this they said in Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah: Everyone must say, “When will my deeds reach the deeds of my fathers?” According to the level of his own soul, included within the soul of the fathers, he can reach this level of slaying the inclination. Concerning it the Sages said, “Whoever sacrifices his inclination …,” as they said in Vayikra Rabbah that the thanksgiving offering does not cease in the future. This is for the slaying of the inclination that will occur in the future, as stated at the end of Sukkah.
records.explanation: Kometz identifies a specific deliverance for which future thanksgiving remains: the removal of the evil inclination. This directly develops Rav Tzadok’s distinction between offerings needed during damage and gratitude for having emerged from it. The comparison concerns the inner reason for continuing thanksgiving, not a new practical ruling about future Temple service.

records.targetHebrew: וכדאיתא בזוה"ק (פקודי רל"ט.) אצל קרבנות רעותא דקרבנא מטיא עד אין סוף בכל זאת עיקר העבודה הוא כמאמרם ז"ל בגמ' (זבחים מ"ו:) לשם השם וכו' לשם מי שאמר והי' העולם וכו' היינו לרצון הבורא ית' שרצה בהוית העולם ובאלו הלבושין כי לאין סוף שהוא אתר דלא אתיידע לא שייך עבודה אלא שאנו עובדים לשם הנחת רוח מי שאמר ונעשה רצונו כלומר שאנו עושין זה העבודה לפי שהוא צוה וכך הוא רצונו באלו הלבושים ע"כ אנו עובדין אותו באלו הלבושים. אבל באמת השי"ת מצדו אינו צריך לכל אלו הלבושים.
records.targetEnglish: The holy Zohar says concerning offerings that the will of the offering reaches to the Infinite. Nevertheless, the essential service follows the Sages’ statement: “For the sake of the Name … for the sake of the One who spoke and the world came to be.” That is, it is directed to the Creator’s will, which desired the world’s existence and these garments. Service does not apply to the Infinite, the place that cannot be known. Rather, we serve for the satisfaction of the One who spoke and whose will was done: we perform this service because He commanded it and this is His will in these garments. Therefore we serve Him through these garments. In truth, from His own side God does not need any of these garments.
records.explanation: Sod distinguishes the satisfaction of God’s freely chosen relationship with creation from a need in the Infinite itself. This gives precision to Rav Tzadok’s “as it were”: human bitterness and repair matter within that relationship, and the libation expresses its restored joy. The target does not state that wine or offerings existed only after Adam’s sin; that temporal claim remains the origin’s own argument.

records.themeTitle: The myrtle signifies good whose full expression is still ahead
records.themeSummary: The section concludes that myrtle and the sanctified cup strengthen the person troubled by weekday life. The covenantal root supports hope even while complete clarification is still needed.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶהוּ "בְּחַמְרָא גּוֹ כָסָא" – שֶׁהוּא לְיַשֵּׁר הַלֵּב וּלְשַׂמְּחוֹ, "וּמְדָאנֵי אָסָא" – שֶׁבָּאוּ לְהוֹרוֹת עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים", כֵּיוָן דְּאִתְגְּזַר אִקְרֵי צַדִּיק. וְעַל יְדֵי שְׁמִירַת שַׁבָּת אֲפִילּוּ עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כֶּאֱנוֹשׁ מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ; וּבַמְּכִילְתָּא: "'שֹׁמֵר שַׁבָּת מֵחַלְּלוֹ וְשֹׁמֵר יָדוֹ וְגוֹמֵר' – שֶׁהַמְשַׁמֵּר שַׁבָּת מְשׁוּמָּר מִן הָעֲבֵירָה", וּבִפְרִי עֵץ חַיִּים: שֶׁנִּיצוֹל מִקִּטְרוּג הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, בְּוַדַּאי כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל צַדִּיקִים. וְזֶהוּ "לַאֲרוּס וַאֲרוּסָה לְאִתְקָפָא חַלָּשִׁין" – מַה שֶּׁחָלַשׁ דַּעְתָּם מִימֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה שֶׁעָבְרוּ בְּטִרְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְעַל יְדֵי הַיַּיִן קִדּוּשׁ וּמְדָאנֵי אָסָא נִתְחַזֵּק וּמִתְיַישֵּׁר הַלֵּב.
records.originEnglish: This is “with wine within the cup”—to straighten the heart and gladden it—“and bunches of myrtle,” which indicate what is said of Israel, “Your people are all righteous,” for one who is circumcised is called righteous. Through observing Shabbat, even one who worships idols like Enosh is forgiven. The Mekhilta states: “‘Who guards Shabbat from profaning it and guards his hand …’—one who guards Shabbat is guarded from transgression.” Pri Etz Chaim says that he is saved from the evil inclination’s accusation. Certainly, then, all Israel are righteous. This is “for groom and bride, to strengthen the weak”: those whose spirit was weakened by the days of action spent in this world’s troubles. Through the sanctified wine and bunches of myrtle, the heart is strengthened and straightened.
records.targetHebrew: וענף עץ עבות מורה, כמו דאיתא במדרש (רבה אמור ל') שיש בו ריח ולא טעם. טעם מורה במקום שכבר מבורר כולו לטוב, אבל זה מורה שאין עדיין מבורר, ורק עתיד להתברר ולאדם טוב מטעימין לו מפרי מעשיו בעוה"ז, אבל שירגיש טעם בעבודתו אין לו עדיין. וזה מורה שיש לו ריח, כמו שאיתא בש"ס (ברכות מ"ג:) איזה דבר שהנשמה נהנת ממנו ולא הגוף, הוי אומר זה הריח, והיינו מאחר שבישראל יש בו חלק אלהי ממעל, ממילא בטח עתיד להתברר לטוב, אבל לעת עתה אינו מבורר עדיין, כי במקום שהוא מבורר כולו לטוב, זה מורה אתרוג. אבל ענף עץ עבות, מורה שאינו מבורר עדיין כולו לטוב.
records.targetEnglish: “A branch of a thick-leaved tree” indicates what the Midrash says: it has fragrance but no taste. Taste indicates a place where everything is already clarified for good. This, however, indicates that it is not yet clarified, but is destined to be clarified. A good person is given a taste of the fruits of his deeds in this world, but this person [represented by the myrtle] does not yet experience taste in his service. This is what having fragrance indicates, as the Talmud says: “What is something the soul enjoys but the body does not? Fragrance.” Since an Israelite has a divine portion from above, he will certainly eventually be clarified for good. At present, however, he is not yet clarified. Where everything is clarified for good is indicated by the etrog; the branch of a thick-leaved tree indicates that he is not yet entirely clarified for good.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef gives the myrtle’s reassurance a precise limit. Fragrance indicates the soul’s good and the promise of clarification, while the lack of taste acknowledges that the work is not yet fully manifest. This illuminates how Rav Tzadok can use myrtle to strengthen a person after troubled weekdays without needing to deny the person’s unfinished state.
